text:
The Tide Chart

By the third week of the residency, Ines had learned to tell time by the light on Marta's desk. Marta wrote at night, and her window, directly across the courtyard from Ines's, glowed a low amber until two, sometimes three. Ines, who rose early to work on her sculpture in the barn, would pass Marta's closed door each morning and feel, briefly, like someone walking past a chapel.

The residency—an old estate on the northern coast, bequeathed by a reclusive ceramist to an arts foundation—housed eight fellows at a time. By late August, six had left. What remained were Ines and Marta, and so the scheduled "final excursion," normally a minibus affair, became a borrowed station wagon and a cooler of sandwiches that the housekeeper, Catarina, made with an air of blessing a voyage.

"You'll miss the good tide if you leave after nine," Catarina said. It was eight forty-five. She handed them a tide chart, the low-water window circled in red marker. "The caves. You can only walk in at low tide. Don't be romantic about it. The sea does not care."

Ines drove. Marta navigated, which meant she held the map upside down and narrated the landscape instead. "That church is where my grandmother was baptized," she said, though Ines was fairly certain they were two hundred kilometers from anywhere Marta's grandmother had been. Marta did this—invented histories for places, for objects, for the sheep in the fields. The other fellows had found it enchanting, then exhausting. Ines had simply found it. Marta was a thing Ines kept finding.

The coast road wound through pine and then opened, without warning, onto the sea. They both made a sound—some involuntary vowel—and then laughed at themselves for making it.

The beach was not the postcard one. This one was reached by a path down a cliff face, the kind established by goats and optimistically adopted by people. Halfway down, Ines's sandal caught a root and she slid three meters on one hip, coming to rest against a boulder with the cooler intact and her dignity elsewhere.

"Are you hurt?" Marta asked, arriving in a controlled crouch, and the question was so carefully neutral that Ines understood, with a small interior lurch, that Marta was managing something. They had been managing things all month. They had managed to sit together at dinner without sitting too close. They had managed to lend each other books with notes in the margins that were about the books. They had managed, the previous Saturday, after three bottles of vinho verde, to stand in the courtyard at midnight saying goodnight for forty minutes, and to say only goodnight.

"Just my pride," Ines said.

"Your pride will recover. It's done it before."

"How would you know?"

"I've watched you fall off that ladder in the barn twice," Marta said. "You always check first if anyone saw."

The beach was wide and empty and held a quality of light Ines had been failing to reproduce in clay for six years—a gray-gold, a luminosity that came from nowhere and everywhere. Marta took off her shoes immediately, with the solemnity of someone entering water or a temple. Ines set down the cooler and thought about saying something and did not say it. This was the texture of the whole month: the unsaid thing had become so large it was practically furniture.

They walked toward the caves. The tide chart said they had until one-fifteen. It was eleven.

"In my novel," Marta said, "there's a scene like this. Two people at the end of something. A beach. I could never get it right."

"What's wrong with it?"

"They talk too much. People at the end of things don't talk. They just—" She stopped, bent to pick up a shell, examined it as though it had interrupted her. "They just stand near each other. And the reader is supposed to understand everything from the standing."

"And does the reader?"

"The reader understands what the reader has lost," Marta said. "That's all reading is."

Ines thought about this the way she thought about Marta's window at night: as a lit thing she was not invited into. She was leaving Thursday, for Lisbon and then home, back to a studio sublet that expired in October. Marta was leaving Friday, for a teaching job in a city Ines kept forgetting the name of, which was perhaps deliberate.

The caves were reached around a headland, the entrance a low arch the sea was already beginning to lick at. Inside, the sound changed—every footstep returned doubled—and the light came in green and trembling off the water pooled on the stone floor. Marta walked in first, and for a moment neither of them said anything, because the cave had the acoustics of a held breath.

"My grandmother's church," Marta whispered, and grinned.

"It's better."

"It's not hers, so it couldn't be."

They went as far in as the dry stone allowed. On the far wall someone had scratched initials, decades of them, one generation atop another, and Marta read them aloud like a liturgy: J.P. + M., 1974. RUI. TINO E LENA. She touched none of them. She had, Ines had noticed, a strict ethics about things that weren't hers.

"We should go back," Ines said, though she didn't move. The water had risen a hand's width since they'd entered.

"We should," Marta agreed, also not moving. And then, with the air of someone setting down a weight she had carried a long way: "My flight isn't Friday. I told them Friday because Friday sounded—decisive. It's actually next Tuesday. I have five days of nowhere in particular."

The cave dripped. The sea said its one word.

"I have four," Ines said. "Days of nowhere."

"Well," Marta said. "Four, then. We'd have four."

And that was all. No one crossed the wet stone. But something in the air pressure of the cave changed, the way it does before weather, and when they walked back out into the light they walked closer together than the path required.

They ate Catarina's sandwiches on the beach, side by side on the driftwood, watching the water climb back over everything they had walked on. The caves were gone by one-thirty. The sea had not cared, exactly as advertised, and there was something satisfying in that—a schedule kept, a law obeyed. Marta ate with her eyes closed, the way she did when food was good, and Ines watched the horizon and let herself think, for the first time in a month, about Thursday without flinching.

"Will you write about this?" Ines asked.

"Probably. Badly, at first. Then in ten years I'll get it right and no one will know it's true."

"Will I know?"

Marta opened her eyes. "You'll know," she said. "I'll make sure you know."

On the drive back, the car broke down. Of course it did—the station wagon belonged to the foundation and had the temperament of an endowment: old, under-funded, resentful. It died at a roundabout outside a fishing village, and they sat in it in the ticking silence, and then Marta began to laugh, and Ines began to laugh, and it was the kind of laughter that has very little to do with the situation and everything to do with the person you're trapped in it with.

A mechanic came. His name was Álvaro, perhaps seventy, and he looked at the engine the way a doctor looks at an old friend, and he told them it would take an hour, and that there was a café. They went to the café. It had a television showing football and a pastry case of considerable ambition, and they sat at a plastic table and drank two espressos each because there was nowhere to be, nowhere on earth, until Álvaro said otherwise.

"Tell me something true," Marta said, stirring her second cup. "Since we're at the end of the world."

"I've been awake at three, many nights," Ines said. "Your light is on. I always think: she's in there making something. And I go back to sleep easier. That's the true thing. It sounds like nothing. It's not nothing."

Marta looked down at her cup for a long moment. "My light is on because I can't sleep," she said. "I sit at the desk and I look at your window and it's dark, and I think: she's in there resting. And I try again. You're the reason I try again. So."

"So."

"We've been keeping each other company," Marta said, "from opposite windows. Like idiots. Like a novel I'd reject."

Álvaro's son came to fetch them at four. The car ran, more or less, and they drove back along the coast as the light went long and copper, the pines blackening against it. They didn't speak much. There was nothing to manage anymore. The thing that had been furniture had, at some point between the cave and the café, become a window with the light left on.

At the estate, Catarina had left soup on the stove and a note about breakfast and, beneath the note, the tide chart, still bearing its red circle. Ines stood in the kitchen holding it while Marta washed their cups.

"She circled the window," Ines said. "The low-water window."

"She's a novelist," Marta said. "She just doesn't know it."

Upstairs, they said goodnight in the hallway, and this time it took only a minute, because it was no longer an ending—it was an intermission, which is a different word entirely. Ines lay in the dark and listened. Across the courtyard, at eleven, the amber light came on. She looked at it for a while. Then she got up, switched on her own lamp, and sat in the window, and across the way she saw Marta's silhouette rise from the desk, and stand, and stay there, two lit rooms facing each other over the dark like an answer.

They had four days. The sea did not care. But the tide came in and went out on a schedule you could print and circle in red, and they had decided, without quite saying so, to learn it.
